## Why This Is Asked

Tests understanding of crash-safe memory allocators for persistent memory, including durable data structures, memory ordering, and recovery mechanisms.

## Key Concepts

- Persistent memory semantics and flush/barrier instructions
- Atomic operations (CAS) on a shared free list
- Crash-recovery journaling and idempotent replay
- Per-thread caches to reduce contention
- Memory ordering constraints and cache line alignment

## Code Example

```javascript
// API usage example demonstrates practical implementation
const allocator = new PMEMAllocator(arena);
const block = allocator.alloc();  // Returns 128-byte block
allocator.free(block);           // Returns block to free list
```

## Follow-up Questions

- How would you extend this design to support variable block sizes?
- What optimizations would you add for high-concurrency scenarios?
- How would you handle fragmentation over time?

## Why This Is Asked
Tests understanding of crash‑consistent data structures in persistent memory, including proper ordering, flush/fence semantics, and recovery guarantees in a high‑throughput path.

## Key Concepts
- Persistent memory semantics and flush instructions (CLWB, CLFLUSHOPT, SFENCE)
- Two‑phase commit for durability
- Ring buffer invariants and recovery in power loss scenarios

## Code Example
```c
// Pseudo-code: writers publish after durable tail update
slot = tail & (N-1);
memcpy(slot_data(slot), payload, 64);
clwb(slot_data(slot));
clwb(&slot_seq(slot)); // update after data
sfence();
slot_seq(slot) = new_seq; // durable publish
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you extend to multiple producers and a multi‑consumer model with minimal contention?
- How would you validate durability guarantees under sudden power loss and after hot restarts?
